title: Gymnasium go-ahead and King Street tower deferral
subtitle: Imperial Oil site deferred to March 3, renoviction report stays on June timeline, heritage permit, appointments, dog designation, OLT settlement authority
overview: Council voted to start phase one of a new gymnasium at the Kitchener Indoor Recreation Complex at Schlegel Park {{vote:m1}}. Staff will use the $19,913,529 in debenture financing approved in September 2024, which staff said is recovered from development charges rather than property taxes. Council will keep lobbying the federal and provincial governments for grants to finish phase two. Supporters said waiting would raise costs and delay opening.

Council deferred the proposed 586-unit, two-tower development at 4611 King Street East to the March 3, 2025 meeting {{vote:m2}}. Staff will keep talking with the applicant about building height, traffic, site access, amenities and parking. The applicant also agreed not to appeal for lack of a decision in the meantime.

Council heard from many tenants and advocates who asked for a renoviction by-law sooner. A motion to reconsider the earlier direction, which would have allowed an earlier staff report, did not get the two-thirds support it needed. Staff expect to report to a Standing Committee on June 2, 2025.

Council also approved a heritage permit for 107 Courtland Avenue East, two Heritage Kitchener appointments, and a changed dog designation. After a closed session, Council authorized settlement negotiations in an Ontario Land Tribunal case.

decisions.detail: Staff will build phase one of the two-phase gymnasium at Schlegel Park using the previously authorized $19,913,529 in debentures and keep seeking senior-government grants for phase two.
The official plan and zoning amendments for the Imperial Oil Limited c/o LJM Developments proposal were deferred to March 3, 2025 for more talks on height, traffic, access, amenities and parking.

The city-initiated official plan and zoning changes were deferred to May 26, 2025 or sooner, to allow a site visit and further talks on land use, transportation, environment and source water protection.
Council approved replacing 22 front-façade windows and the main entrance doors under the Ontario Heritage Act.
Preston Arens and Nic E'Silva were appointed to the Heritage Kitchener Committee for a term ending November 15, 2026.
Council ratified the appeal committee's decision to change the dog 'Murphy' from Dangerous Dog to Potentially Dangerous Dog, with modified conditions.
The City Solicitor may enter settlement negotiations in OLT case OLT-22-002377, and the General Manager of Development Services may approve and sign any settlement.

debate: On the gymnasium, delegates from sport hosting, volleyball and basketball said there is not enough court space, that clubs turn away players, and that tournaments bring significant economic activity. Staff warned that waiting would add millions in cost, citing tariff risk.

Several councillors supporting the gym stressed that it is only a shell until grants arrive. One said they would not approve the full gym on the city's own, and asked residents to press their MPs and MPPs. Staff noted debt-related risks: possible changes to development charge rules, cancelled grant programs, and a tighter reserve if little grant money arrives.

On King Street East, nearby residents opposed the towers over privacy, traffic and U-turn safety, no nearby parks or grocery stores, a 990-metre walk to transit, and the fact that the site is outside the transit station area. Some councillors shared these concerns. Others worried that a refusal could be appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal, which staff said often favours developers, and that the reduced height and 10 affordable units could be lost.

The applicant said the revised plan cuts units, keeps 493 parking spaces and offers 10 affordable units. A councillor and the applicant disagreed on whether 10 units was enough, and some councillors asked for about 20. Several councillors also noted that the residents' detailed recommendations arrived only that day.

On renovictions, tenants described personal hardship and urged council to pass a by-law sooner. Staff said a by-law would need new staff and budget and that the city is not the housing services manager. Council chose to keep the existing June timeline.
